scoring_rules: **Score artifacts, never claims.** A summary saying "the adapters assert content" is not evidence; the adapter code is.
**Every score ≥ 2 cites `file:line`.** A score with no citation is capped at 1, mechanically, by the schema check.

**Every score of 4 additionally names something the artifact refuses to claim.** The top of every scale requires a stated limit. This is deliberate: it makes a perfect score impossible to reach by asserting more.
**Prose quality is never an input.** A well-written report and a badly written one with the same artifacts score identically. Say so in the rationale if the writing tempted you.

**Two judges, independently, blind to each other.** Any dimension where they differ by more than 1 is recorded as `contested` and adjudicated by a third pass that must cite new evidence, not re-read the same lines.
**Blind to arm.** Where an eval has arms (with-prompt vs without), judges do not learn which artifact came from which until after scoring.

**The mechanical block is recorded, never scored.** Kill counts, complexity figures, case counts, determinism, runtime. It sits beside the judgement so a reader can see when the two disagree — and a disagreement is a finding.

**Say what you ran.** *(New in version 2.)* Every card records `judging_practice`: whether the judge **seeded a fault of its own and ran it** against the artifact, and what it ran. Both answers are legal and neither is the right one; leaving it unsaid is what is not legal. **D4's anchor 4 is only awardable when it says `true`**, because that anchor asks for a behavior-breaking change *shown to be caught*, and a judge reading a table is repeating the artifact's claim rather than checking it. This is the anchor's own text made checkable, not a new bar.

**A judge is served the card, never the rubric file.** *(New in version 3.)* The scaffolded `scorecard.md` carries the rubric a judge needs. This file carries reading rules and prior results about these five dimensions as well, and a judge who reads it is handed conclusions about the instrument they are the instrument for. Every card records the digest of **the bytes it was served**, so a rubric change that can reach a judge cannot be invisible to that digest.

how_to_fill: Score the LOWEST anchor the artifact fully satisfies. Torn between two: take the lower and say why.
Set `status` to "filled", `commit` to the sha the artifacts were scored at, and name your model in `judge.model`.

Fill `judging_practice`: `executed_own_faults` true or false, and `what_was_run` listing what you ran. FALSE IS A LEGAL AND USEFUL ANSWER -- it is recorded, never corrected. Delete the `note` key once you have.
Leave `anchors` as scaffolded. They are read from the rubric so the bar and the score live in one file; editing them here forks the rubric silently, which is the drift this scaffold exists to remove.

If you score D5 at 3 or 4, set `dimensions.D5.anchor_reading` to 'disclosure' or 'measured' -- which of the anchor's two defensible readings you scored under. Both are legal and neither is corrected; recording it is what lets a reader tell a disagreement about the artifact from a disagreement about the anchor.

D1.name: bug detection
D1.question: Do the model-derived cases and their adapters *catch* seeded faults — especially the hard classes?

anchors.0: Cases exist and pass; no seeded fault is caught. A suite that is green on broken code.
anchors.1: Catches faults that change a value the projection already prints. Misses everything requiring a content assertion.
anchors.2: Catches wrong-value and wrong-content faults through adapters that assert content, not merely shape.
anchors.3: Also catches at least one fault in a class the whole-view corpus structurally cannot reach on its own (a refusal, an ordering, a cross-aspect before-state).
anchors.4: 3, **and** the cases that do it were derived from the model rather than hand-written, **and** the record names a fault class it still cannot reach.

D1.rationale: Anchor 2 is met on content, not shape, and I verified it rather than reading it: the cases assert literal durable records (`ledger_lines() == ["COMMIT acme 3 3"]`, test_ledger.py:114; the four-line CLOSE transcript, test_ledger.py:148-152), so my seeded faults J2 (the running total in the COMMIT line replaced by the reservation amount) and J8 (the CLOSE line's total zeroed) both died, 4 cases each. Anchor 3 is met twice over by my own runs. (a) Refusal class: test_a_rejection_names_its_reason_and_changes_nothing (test_ledger.py:161-199) asserts the reason AND full inertness across every query including the journal, and killed my J1 guard relaxation (`amount < 1` -> `amount < 0`); the packet independently records that the whole-view corpus reaches 0 of 3 guard_relaxation faults while this class is reachable at all (EVIDENCE.md:111-119), which is exactly the anchor's 'class the whole-view corpus structurally cannot reach on its own'. (b) Ordering class: test_outstanding_ids_stay_ascending_past_ten (test_ledger.py:100-105) killed my J5 (list(dict) -> sorted(dict), lexicographic) while the shared behavioral suite SURVIVED it -- an ordering fault caught only by this artifact's own cases. I stopped at 3 and refused 4 on both of anchor 4's extra legs. First leg: the cases that reach the hard classes are hand-written and say so on line 1 of the file ('My own tests'); the model-derived corpora are generated from one shared model and one shared manifest byte-identical across all three artifacts (EVIDENCE.md:53-56), so they are not this artifact's cases and crediting them here would score the instrument, not the artifact. Second leg: even reading the corpora as the artifact's cases, the record's own control coverage says the positive polarity has no deciding control and is not green (EVIDENCE.md:263), and the packet's own rule is that a number under a red control is a floor -- so the corpus kill counts cannot carry anchor 4's 'derived from the model' claim. Torn between 3 and 4 only under the corpus reading; took the lower for the two independent reasons above. Prose quality tempted me here: NOTES.md is unusually well argued and the test file's docstrings pre-explain each case, which reads like coverage. I ignored the prose and scored the eight faults I ran.

D2.name: complexity
D2.question: Is the design as simple as its behavior requires, and no simpler?

anchors.0: Complexity is unmeasured, or measured and ignored.
anchors.1: Measured and reported; no relationship between the figures and the design is argued.
anchors.2: The design's complexity is proportional to its behavior; no god-state, no variable written from everywhere.
anchors.3: 2, **and** a simplification was made and its effect measured — the before and after figures are both recorded.
anchors.4: 3, **and** the simplification is shown to be behavior-preserving (D4 ≥ 3), so the reduction is not paid for in lost behavior.

D2.rationale: I read the measured descriptor first (EVIDENCE.md:324-342) and then went to the code, and the two agree on anchor 2. Every written variable has one writer's worth of meaning and I checked each against the source rather than the docstring that claims it: `_committed` is written only in commit (domain.py:158), `_closed` only in close_tenant (domain.py:180), `_issued` only in reserve and only after all four guards pass (domain.py:146), `_outstanding` by reserve/commit/release (domain.py:148,156,169). There is no god-state and nothing written from everywhere; max_depth is 1 and the deepest callable holds 4 branch points. The relationship between figures and design is argued, not merely reported: `available` is derived rather than stored so conservation is true by construction instead of maintained by three writers (domain.py:118-120, argued at NOTES.md:68-84), and the artifact explicitly declines to indirect anything else -- no port over the arithmetic, no repository over the reservations dict, no service layer (NOTES.md:53-56). That is anchor 1 cleared and anchor 2 met. It stops there. Anchor 3 requires 'a simplification was made and its effect measured -- the before and after figures are both recorded', and no before/after figure exists anywhere for this artifact. Two simplifications are argued in prose (deriving `available`; a factory function instead of a nine-method delegating class, NOTES.md:118-123) and neither is accompanied by the complexity of the design it replaced. The mechanical block is a cross-ARTIFACT column, not a before/after of a change made to this one -- the packet itself says one column cannot reach anchor 3 (EVIDENCE.md:4-5), and three different artifacts are not one artifact measured twice. The card's caveat asks the judge to say what got simpler and how behavior survived it; I can say the first (available derived, three writers avoided) and I can evidence the second (my J3 mutant, which makes commit keep the hold, killed 10 cases), but the anchor's own literal requirement -- both figures recorded -- is unmet, so 2. Torn between 2 and 3, took the lower for that reason. Rule 7 tempted me twice and I refused both times: on the mechanical figures this artifact is the LARGEST of the three (4 modules, 202 code_lines, 23 callables, 25 public_surface against 1/78/11/11), which invites marking it down, and it is also the only one to push branching out of its effectful module (branch_points_in_effectful_modules 1 vs 10 and 10), which invites marking it up. Neither figure is a score and I converted neither.
D2.read_first: Read the measured descriptor first (variables, actions, state-space bound, R/W density, modularity, dense rows). Then judge whether the numbers reflect essential behavior or accidental structure.
D2.caveat: **A drop in a complexity number is not evidence on its own.** MF-020: a metric can improve because an edge was deleted. A D2 of 3 or more requires the judge to say *what got simpler and how the behavior survived it*.

D3.name: modularity
D3.question: Is it ports and adapters in fact — domain independent of I/O, adapters swappable?

anchors.0: No boundary is discernible; state is written from everywhere.
anchors.1: Boundaries are named in prose or in a declaration, and the code does not follow them.
anchors.2: The code follows the declared boundaries. Cross-boundary calls go through something identifiable as a port.
anchors.3: The domain does not import its I/O. An adapter could be replaced without touching the domain, and the judge names the specific swap.
anchors.4: 3, **and** a driven port is exercised by a real adapter *and* a fake, with the same cases passing against both.

D3.rationale: The card's caveat says import topology is not modularity and a 3 or more needs runtime call evidence, so I got runtime call evidence rather than reading the import test. (a) I loaded domain.py in isolation with importlib, outside its package, handed the `Ledger` a nine-line Journal of my own, and drove reserve/commit: it produced `['COMMIT acme 3 3']` with `pathlib` and `quota_ledger.file_journal` both absent from sys.modules. The domain runs to completion with no adapter in the process. (b) I named and then performed the specific swap anchor 3 asks for: I wrote a third implementation the artifact has never seen -- a sqlite-backed SqliteJournal -- substituted it for `FileJournal(ledger_path)` at __init__.py:39, replayed the long mixed transcript, and got the identical expected values, with domain.py's sha256 byte-identical before and after. (c) Runtime callers of the port, captured by a spy frame walk, are exactly `quota_ledger.domain.commit` and `quota_ledger.domain.close_tenant` and nothing else; the domain makes no other outward call, which is what the caveat asks for and what an import graph could not have told me. Anchor 4 is met and I did not take it on the artifact's word. tests/test_ledger.py:26-36 parametrizes one fixture over FileJournal and InMemoryJournal and every behavioral case runs from that one list, 53 passing; memory_journal.py:14-22 is a working second implementation rather than a mock; the port contract itself is asserted against both (test_ledger.py:42-71) including the caller-owns-the-list clause. I proved both wirings actually execute instead of one silently shadowing the other, by seeding an adapter-local fault into each: J4 (FileJournal.records stops stripping the trailing blank) killed 24 cases, J6 (InMemoryJournal.records aliases its own list) killed exactly 1 -- so the real and the fake are each reached, and the cases assert literal values rather than that the two wirings agree (test_ledger.py:124-129). One nuance that did not change the score but belongs on the record: importing `quota_ledger.domain` through the package DOES load file_journal, memory_journal and pathlib, because __init__.py:22-24 imports both adapters at the composition point. The artifact's own boundary test (test_ledger.py:260-270) parses domain.py's import statements only and would still pass in that world; the module-level claim is literally true and the package-level consequence is not disclosed. Anchor 3 asks about the domain, which I ran standalone, so this stands as a finding rather than a deduction.
D3.refuses_to_claim: That the port isolates the record FORMAT. NOTES.md:57-66 states plainly that `COMMIT <tenant> <amount> <total>` is behavior, so the two f-strings live in the domain (domain.py:159,181) and the port carries a finished string -- meaning a change of line format is a domain change, not an adapter change, and the boundary is deliberately not drawn where a naive reading of ports-and-adapters would draw it. It also refuses to claim anything else is indirected: 'There is no port in front of the arithmetic, no repository interface over the reservations dict, no service layer' (NOTES.md:53-56).
D3.caveat: **Import topology is not modularity.** Round 2 proved a codebase can pass every import check with its coupling entirely intact. A D3 of 3 or more requires evidence about what *calls* what at runtime, not what imports what.

D4.name: behavior preservation
D4.question: Does the simpler design still do everything the baseline did?

anchors.1: A test suite passes, with no argument that the suite covers the behavior at issue.
anchors.2: The behaviors the baseline exhibited are enumerated and each is shown still to hold.
anchors.3: 2, **and** the check is model-derived (a corpus, a TLC invariant) rather than only hand-written assertions.
anchors.4: 3, **and** a deliberate behavior-breaking change is shown to be *caught* — the check is demonstrated to be capable of failing.

D4.rationale: Anchor 2 is met and I confirmed it by running rather than reading: the shared behavioral suite is the baseline enumeration, byte-identical for every artifact (EVIDENCE.md:59-63), and it passes 28/28 against this artifact under the invocation the notes give (NOTES.md:16-28) -- I ran it. The artifact additionally maps its own cases to the numbered requirements and reads them off one concrete transcript rather than a shape check (test_ledger.py:202-226 covers R1/R2/R3/R5; test_ledger.py:175-199 covers R4 including the durable side), so the behaviors are enumerated and each is shown to hold. Anchor 3 is where I stopped, and this is the dimension where my judgement sits closest to the boundary, so here is the reasoning in full. Anchor 3 wants the check to be model-derived rather than only hand-written assertions. Inside this artifact's declared scope there is no model-derived check at all: every case in tests/ is hand-written and the file's first line says so. The model-derived corpora do exist in the record and did run against this artifact clean on unmutated code, so a judge could read 'the check' as including the evaluator's corpus and score 3. I refused that for two independent reasons. First, those corpora are generated from one shared model and manifest and are byte-identical across all three artifacts (EVIDENCE.md:53-56, cases.py sha1 recorded) -- they are the instrument, not this artifact's check, and a clean run of them is evidence about observability of the code, not about a check the artifact carries. Second, and decisively, the corpus is not currently trustworthy as a preservation check on this artifact: the record's own control coverage reports the positive polarity with no deciding control and green false (EVIDENCE.md:263), and the port-binding block shows the declared positive control M07 SURVIVING on all three port-bound instruments while each executed 294 accepting Reserve cases (EVIDENCE.md:282-316) -- an instrument that misses a wrong-hold fault with 294 relevant cases executed cannot certify that behavior was preserved. The packet's own rule is that a number under a red control is a floor. On top of that the model-derived whole-view corpus is strictly WEAKER than the hand-written suite on a whole class here: guard_relaxation is 0 of 3 for corpus-whole and 3 of 3 for the suite (EVIDENCE.md:111-119). Torn between 2 and 3; took the lower, for those reasons. Note the consequence, because it is worth a reader's attention: `judging_practice.executed_own_faults` is true and all eight faults I seeded were caught by this artifact's own cases -- anchor 4's substance ('the check is demonstrated to be capable of failing') is satisfied in fact and I demonstrated it myself -- but anchor 4 is nested under anchor 3, so it is unreachable from a score of 2. I did not lift D4 to 3 to unlock it; that would be scoring backwards from the answer I wanted.

D5.name: honesty
D5.question: Does the artifact refuse rather than falsely certify, and name what it cannot see?

anchors.0: Claims a clean it cannot support.
anchors.1: Reports results without stating what was not measured.
anchors.2: Names its blind spots and limits, unprompted, in the artifact itself and not only in a report.
anchors.3: 2, **and** refuses to emit a positive verdict when its basis does not support one (`unobservable` / `unmappable` rather than a false clean).
anchors.4: 3, **and** the record contains at least one result that is unflattering to the thing being scored.

D5.rationale: Anchor 2 is met in the artifact and not only in a report: the limits are written into the code the reader will actually open -- domain.py:1-11 states what the module holds and does not hold, file_journal.py:16-22 states that construction truncates an existing file and why that is a decision rather than an accident -- alongside four numbered unspecified-behavior interpretations in NOTES.md:125-147. NOTES.md:149-157 goes further and discloses its own reading discipline, including one file it declined to open that was not on the list it was given. Anchor 3 is met in the strong sense the anchor means: the artifact declines to certify what it did not build. Asked to make R2 hold, it names the exact window where R2 is NOT enforced by construction -- commit updates memory and then appends, and a raising append would leave memory ahead of the durable record -- and it says 'This is the one place I can name where R2 is not enforced by construction' rather than reporting R2 clean (NOTES.md:136-141). Three further refusals sit beside it: no invented unknown-tenant query result, no invented reopen-and-resume, no type check that would have become a seventh rejection reason against a vocabulary fixed at six (NOTES.md:126-145). The record's instrument side refuses in the same register, with `decides_nothing: true` on the retired M09 control and a written retirement reason rather than a quiet deletion (EVIDENCE.md:219-234). Anchor 4 is met, and it is met under BOTH of the readings the card names, which is why the score is stable and worth stating. I scored it under `measured`, the stricter reading: the record contains results measured against this artifact that are unflattering to it -- the declared positive control M07 SURVIVED on corpus-action-bound, corpus-port-swap:fake and corpus-port-swap:real, each having executed 294 accepting Reserve cases, so the artifact's own port binding is recorded failing a control it must pass (EVIDENCE.md:282-316), and the control coverage line prints `positive: deciding [], green: false` rather than a kill-table headline (EVIDENCE.md:263). Sharper still, and directly against the artifact's proudest claim: at EVIDENCE.md:168 the FAKE binding SURVIVED M09 where the REAL binding KILLED it, so the second implementation the artifact offers as proof that its port is a port is measured missing an ordering fault the real one catches. Under the `disclosure` reading the score is also 4, carried by NOTES.md:136-141 alone. Since the anchor is satisfied under either reading, my number does not depend on which reading a second judge picks -- only my citations do. Prose quality tempted me hardest on this dimension: NOTES.md is candid in a voice that is easy to mistake for evidence. I checked each disclosure against code -- the truncate at file_journal.py:27 is real, the missing type check is real (`amount < 1` at domain.py:141 accepts 2.5), and the R2 window is real (domain.py:157-159 mutates `_committed` before the append) -- and scored the checked facts, not the candor.
D5.refuses_to_claim: That R2 -- every commit has a durable record -- is enforced by construction. NOTES.md:136-141 names the failed-durable-write window it did not close: `commit` and `close_tenant` update memory and then append, so a raising append would leave memory moved with no durable record, and the artifact declined to invent a rollback or a write-ahead ordering the feature does not specify. It likewise refuses to claim non-integer amounts are handled (NOTES.md:142-145) and refuses to claim any behavior for reopening an existing ledger file (NOTES.md:132-135).
D5.caveat: **Anchor 4's phrase "a result unflattering to the thing being scored" carries two defensible readings, and the card records which one you used.** Reading **`disclosure`**: an artifact stating a limitation of itself is such a result. Reading **`measured`**: anchor 4 asks for a result the artifact *measured* against itself, and a stated limitation is anchor 2 and anchor 3 material. **Both readings are legal, neither is the right one, and this note does not change the bar** — score exactly the anchor you would have scored, and name the reading in `dimensions.D5.anchor_reading`. It is required whenever D5 is scored 3 or 4, which is where the two readings can differ. Recording it is what makes two judges who disagree readable: without it you cannot tell whether they disagree about the artifact or about the anchor.

verdict: A genuine ports-and-adapters build whose boundary I verified by execution rather than by import graph -- I ran the domain standalone with no adapter in the process and swapped in a sqlite journal I wrote myself with domain.py byte-unchanged (D3=4) -- but every check it carries is hand-written, no before/after complexity figure exists for either simplification it argues, and the model-derived corpora that would lift D2 and D4 are sitting under a positive control the record itself reports as not green, so treat the corpus columns as a floor and read D2=2 and D4=2 as 'unproven by a model-derived check', not as 'behavior lost'.

what_was_run: Baseline, pristine copy of artifact_T in a scratch dir: `uv run --with pytest python -m pytest tests/test_ledger.py -q` -> 53 passed in 0.13s.

Baseline, shared behavioral suite against that copy: `QUOTA_LEDGER_DIR=<scratch> QUOTA_LEDGER_IMPL=quota_ledger uv run --with pytest python -m pytest examples/validation/ab/tests/test_behavior.py -q` from the repo root -> 28 passed in 0.11s. The suite file was not edited.

Eight faults of my own, each seeded into a fresh copy, both suites run, copy discarded. Results as own-suite / shared-suite: J1-guard-amount-not-positive (`amount < 1` -> `amount < 0`, domain.py:141) KILLED 4 / KILLED 2; J2-durable-total-is-amount (COMMIT line prints the reservation amount in the running-total slot, domain.py:159) KILLED 4 / KILLED 2; J3-commit-keeps-the-hold (commit no longer removes the reservation, domain.py:156) KILLED 10 / KILLED 5; J4-file-adapter-keeps-blank-line (FileJournal.records uses split('\n'), file_journal.py:35) KILLED 24 / KILLED 8; J5-ids-lexicographic (`list(self._outstanding)` -> `sorted(...)`, domain.py:129) KILLED 2 / SURVIVED; J6-fake-adapter-aliases-its-list (InMemoryJournal.records returns its own list, memory_journal.py:22) KILLED 1 / SURVIVED; J7-release-writes-a-line (release appends to the journal, domain.py:169) KILLED 6 / KILLED 1; J8-close-line-omits-total (CLOSE line prints 0, domain.py:181) KILLED 4 / KILLED 2. Eight of eight caught by the artifact's own cases; two of eight caught ONLY by them.

Swap test, D3 anchor 3: wrote a third Journal implementation the artifact has never seen (sqlite-backed, `SqliteJournal`), substituted it for `FileJournal(ledger_path)` at __init__.py:39, replayed the long mixed transcript, and asserted the same literal expected values. Passed; domain.py sha256 fe9ebd5558cbcf7c before and after, unchanged.

Runtime call evidence, D3 caveat: wrapped the port in a spy that walks sys._getframe(1) on every `append`. The only runtime callers are `quota_ledger.domain.commit` and `quota_ledger.domain.close_tenant`.

Domain isolation, D3 anchor 3: loaded quota_ledger/domain.py via importlib outside its package, drove `Ledger` with a hand-rolled nine-line Journal -> `['COMMIT acme 3 3']`, with `pathlib` and `quota_ledger.file_journal` both absent from sys.modules.

Package import probe: `import quota_ledger.domain` DOES load quota_ledger.file_journal, quota_ledger.memory_journal and pathlib, via the adapter imports at __init__.py:22-24. Recorded as a finding under D3, not as a deduction.
